title: The Execution System
hook: Orange vests by the gate show whether the shift briefing is a loop or just another speech.
counterintuition: A system can sound complete while its parts still drift apart. Execution gets steadier only when action, score, and adjustment stay in one closed loop.
tryThisNow: Draw a three-step loop for one goal: action taken, score seen, adjustment made before the next week starts.
keyTakeaway: See execution as a closed system of recurring disciplines rather than isolated bursts of effort. The standard is visible action, not a better-sounding intention.

The loop matters because a good action that never feeds a score cannot teach the next action what to do.  A loop is useful only when yesterday's evidence changes today's work.

examples.title: Alice closes the shift loop

planSpec.audience: a practitioner in airport ground crew shift planning who needs the chapter move under real pressure
planSpec.stakes: the visible result will slip while everyone can still explain the effort
planSpec.requiredBeat: Beth connects gate briefing, shift score, and correction in one loop.

examples.scenario: Orange vests hang by gate numbers while Alice briefs the airport ground crew. Yesterday's late baggage carts are on the sheet, but no adjustment is listed. She must decide whether the briefing is a speech or a closed loop: action taken, score seen, correction assigned before the first pushback.  Alice writes yesterday's cart delay beside today's gate assignments, then gives one ramp lead the correction before the first pushback.
examples.whatToDo: Make the loop visible in the shift briefing: yesterday's action, today's score, and one correction with an owner before work starts.
examples.whyItMatters: A closed system prevents yesterday's miss from disappearing. Alice makes execution repeatable by forcing feedback back into action.

examples.title: Vincent changes the release train

planSpec.audience: a decision-maker in app security release train choosing whether to protect execution or drift
planSpec.stakes: the next 12 weeks will inherit a soft plan unless the decision is made now
planSpec.requiredBeat: Etienne uses the release train to show action, feedback, adjustment.

examples.scenario: At 10:15 a.m. in the app security room, Vincent studies release branches on a status board. As release lead, he must decide whether failed checks become background noise or the next cycle's correction.  Vincent changes the release checklist from the failed security checks and asks the engineer on call to verify it before the next branch cut.
examples.whatToDo: Use the failed checks as feedback, not noise. Add the correction to the release train before the team rolls forward.
examples.whyItMatters: The release train improves only if failed checks alter the next run. Shipping again without adjustment is effort without learning.

examples.title: Marit blocks the broken scene

planSpec.audience: a team lead in community theater rehearsal calendar who needs visible proof before the week softens
planSpec.stakes: the team will mistake motion for progress if the proof stays hidden
planSpec.requiredBeat: Maja turns rehearsal notes into the next blocked practice.

examples.scenario: You can see costumes tagged by scene across the community theater table. Marit has notes from rehearsal, attendance gaps, and one broken scene change. The cast wants encouragement, but she faces a choice: praise the effort or turn the notes into the next blocked practice.  Marit turns the broken scene-change note into a blocked rehearsal slot and has the stage manager mark whether it improved.
examples.whatToDo: Turn rehearsal notes into a blocked practice for the broken scene change. The system works only when feedback returns as scheduled action.
examples.whyItMatters: Marit keeps the cast from confusing energy with progress. Notes become useful only when they return as practice.

examples.title: Matteo reads the recall data

planSpec.audience: a reflective operator in dental practice recall campaign reading last week's failure as evidence
planSpec.stakes: a repeat failure will be explained away instead of corrected
planSpec.requiredBeat: Pablo links recall calls, visible response, and next week's adjustment.

examples.scenario: At 8:00 a.m. in the dental practice, Matteo holds recall postcards bound with rubber bands. As office owner, he must decide whether the campaign repeats or the response data changes the next batch.  Matteo pairs recall-call volume with response data and changes the patient list before the next batch is assigned.
examples.whatToDo: Pair call volume with response data and adjust the next batch. Matteo needs a loop, not another isolated recall push.
examples.whyItMatters: The recall campaign had action but no learning. Response data gives the next batch a smarter starting point.

examples.title: Nina carries the buyer signal

planSpec.audience: a reader in specialty coffee wholesale route comparing intention before the move with proof after it
planSpec.stakes: the work will stay aspirational unless the action changes in the room
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anya closes the loop from wholesale visit to roast change.

examples.scenario: Sample bags of beans line the cupping table at the specialty coffee roaster. Before, Nina treated each wholesale visit as a separate push. After, she records the buyer response, changes the roast note, and sends the next visit out with yesterday's feedback built in.  Nina adds the buyer signal to the roast note and sends the next wholesale visit out with that change built in.
examples.whatToDo: Record the buyer response and change the roast note before the next visit. Feedback has to alter the next action.
examples.whyItMatters: Nina turns market feedback into changed behavior. Each visit can now compound instead of starting from scratch.

examples.title: Aman turns errors into correction

planSpec.audience: two colleagues in Lisbon fintech compliance pod forcing the commitment into plain speech
planSpec.stakes: a public promise will dissolve unless someone names the proof and owner
planSpec.requiredBeat: Chidi turns compliance review into a repeating execution loop.

examples.scenario: At 5:45 p.m. in the Lisbon fintech pod, Aman opens regulatory folders beside espresso cups. As compliance lead, he must decide whether three filing errors become blame or a closed-loop correction.  Aman assigns the filing-error correction, owner, and next compliance review before the Lisbon pod closes the folders.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the errors as system feedback. Assign the correction, owner, and next review so compliance improves instead of merely producing blame.
examples.whyItMatters: Aman protects ownership without shame. Errors become useful when they close the loop and change the next filing.
